original_question: Fix r > 0. A maximal distance minimizer (also called an r-minimizer) for a compact set M \subset \mathbb{R}^d is a connected compact set \Sigma of minimal length (one-dimensional Hausdorff measure H^1(\Sigma)) among connected compact sets satisfying M \subset B_r(\Sigma), where B_r(\Sigma) is the closed r-neighborhood of \Sigma. Suppose \Sigma is an r-minimizer for some compact set M. Consider the maximal distance minimization problem with target set taken to be B_r(\Sigma). Is \Sigma the unique r-minimizer for B_r(\Sigma)?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1 in Section 1: if \Sigma is an r-minimizer for some compact target M, then \Sigma should be the unique r-minimizer for its own closed r-neighborhood \overline{B_r(\Sigma)}. The nearby context is exactly the known half recorded as Proposition 1.2 (that such a \Sigma is at least an r-minimizer for \overline{B_r(\Sigma)}) and the supporting existence result Theorem 1.3 for injective C^{1,1}-curves and sufficiently small r. ([emergentmind.com](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/maximal-distance-minimizers?utm_source=openai))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right geometric optimization problem, the correct admissible class (connected compact sets minimizing one-dimensional Hausdorff measure), the dependence on a fixed radius r>0, and the exact uniqueness issue obtained by replacing the original target M with the r-neighborhood generated by \Sigma itself. In substance, it is very close to the paper's intended open question.
missing_details: The paper uses the closed r-neighborhood \overline{B_r(\Sigma)}; if you keep the notation B_r(\Sigma), you should say explicitly that it is the closed r-neighborhood.

The universal quantifiers should be explicit: for every ambient dimension d and every compact M\subset\mathbb{R}^d with r>0, if \Sigma is an r-minimizer for (M,r), then ask the uniqueness question for \overline{B_r(\Sigma)}.

Uniqueness should be stated relative to the same admissible class as in the definition: connected compact competitors \Gamma minimizing \mathcal H^1 under the coverage constraint \overline{B_r(\Sigma)}\subset\overline{B_r(\Gamma)}.

To be fully paper-faithful, it helps to separate the known part from the open part: Proposition 1.2 already gives that \Sigma is an r-minimizer for \overline{B_r(\Sigma)}; the conjectural part is uniqueness only.
refined_question: Let d\ge 1, let r>0, and let M\subset\mathbb{R}^d be compact. Suppose \Sigma\subset\mathbb{R}^d is a connected compact set with minimal one-dimensional Hausdorff measure \mathcal H^1 among all connected compact sets \Gamma satisfying M\subset\overline{B_r(\Gamma)}. Must \Sigma be the unique connected compact set of minimal \mathcal H^1 among all connected compact sets \Gamma satisfying \overline{B_r(\Sigma)}\subset\overline{B_r(\Gamma)}? In other words, if \Sigma is an r-minimizer for some compact set M, is \Sigma the unique r-minimizer for its own closed r-neighborhood \overline{B_r(\Sigma)}?
justification: The draft is targeting the paper's inverse-minimizer uniqueness conjecture, not a broader neighboring problem. The paper's surrounding discussion first recalls the already-known fact that any r-minimizer \Sigma for some M is again an r-minimizer for \overline{B_r(\Sigma)}; that is precisely the non-open half of your draft. The open step is then whether this self-induced target has \Sigma as its unique minimizer, which is exactly the content of Conjecture 1.1. Theorem 1.3 is nearby because it provides evidence from the class of injective C^{1,1}-curves, showing that self-neighborhood minimizers do arise in a substantial family. ([huggingface.co](https://huggingface.co/datasets/howey/unarXive/viewer?utm_source=openai))
